title: The Weight of Gold
author: Léxi
desc: Une jeune journaliste d'Abidjan enquête sur une mine d'or clandestine. Plus elle avance, plus la vérité devient dangereuse.

p: Nadège Koffi had been working at *L'Éclaireur*, a small Abidjan newspaper, for barely eight months when she realised that most of her job consisted of rewriting press releases. Ministers inaugurated roads, companies announced record profits, footballers signed contracts — and she turned it all into tidy paragraphs that nobody would remember by Monday.
So when an elderly man walked into the newsroom one rainy Tuesday, clutching a plastic bag as if it contained his entire life, she was the only journalist who bothered to look up.
"I'm looking for someone who isn't afraid," he said.
The editor, Monsieur Dosso, laughed without lifting his eyes from his screen. "Then you've come to the wrong building, old man."

Nadège offered him a chair and a cup of water. His name was Bamba Seydou, and he came from a village near Hiré, in the centre-west of the country. In the plastic bag, there were photographs: a river turned the colour of rust, children with skin rashes, a hillside stripped bare, and dozens of young men digging in muddy pits.

"They came eighteen months ago," he explained. "First a few boys from neighbouring countries, then trucks, then machines. They're looking for gold. They use mercury to separate it from the earth, and they pour what's left into our river. We drink from that river, Madame. Our children bathe in it."
"Have you told the authorities?"

The old man smiled, and the smile was more painful than tears. "I have told everybody. The sub-prefect, the gendarmes, the deputy. Each time, the next week, the machines are still there. Somebody is being paid to look the other way."
That evening, Nadège pitched the story to Monsieur Dosso. He listened with growing irritation.
"Illegal gold mining? Every newspaper has done that story. It doesn't sell."
"Not like this. He says someone important is protecting the site."

Dosso sighed and took off his glasses. "Nadège, you're talented. But talented young journalists who go looking for 'someone important' tend to discover that their careers are much shorter than they expected." He paused. "You have one week. Your own money. And if anything goes wrong, *L'Éclaireur* never sent you."

chapters.t: The River the Colour of Rust
p: The bus to Hiré took seven hours, most of which Nadège spent rereading her notes and wondering whether Dosso had been right. When she finally arrived, Bamba Seydou was waiting for her at the side of the road with a motorbike that seemed older than he was.

The village was quieter than she had imagined. Many houses were empty; their owners, Bamba explained, had left for the mining site, where a single good day could earn a young man more than a month of cocoa farming.
"You can't blame them," he said. "The cocoa price is low, and the gold is right there under their feet. But they don't understand what it costs."

The next morning, before dawn, he took her through the forest to a hill overlooking the site. Nadège had seen photographs, but nothing had prepared her for the scale of it. Hundreds of pits, some of them twenty metres deep, had transformed the landscape into something lunar. Generators roared. Excavators — real, expensive machines, not the shovels of poor diggers — moved earth from one side of the valley to the other. Below them, the river ran thick and orange.
She took photographs with a long lens, her hands trembling slightly. Then she noticed something that made her stop.

Parked near a large tent was a white four-by-four with official plates. And next to it, talking to a man in a cowboy hat, stood a figure she recognised immediately from dozens of press conferences she had covered: Honoré Gnagbo, deputy director of a national agency responsible for — of all things — environmental protection.
"Do you know who that is?" she whispered.
Bamba shook his head.
"He's the man who's supposed to be stopping all this."

Back in Abidjan, Nadège spent three days verifying everything. She found the company registered as the "owner" of the excavators: a firm with no website, no employees and an address that turned out to be a closed hair salon in Marcory. She found that the firm's founding documents had been signed by a certain Laurette Gnagbo. And, after several hours in the archives of the commercial court, she found that Laurette Gnagbo was Honoré Gnagbo's sister-in-law.
On Friday, she wrote the article. It was precise, carefully sourced, and devastating. Dosso read it twice in silence.
"This is real journalism," he said finally. "Which means it's going to cause real problems."
Before publishing, Nadège did what any responsible journalist must do: she called Honoré Gnagbo's office to give him the opportunity to respond. His secretary promised he would call back.
He didn't call back. But that evening, as Nadège was walking home from the bus stop, a black car slowed down beside her. The window opened a few centimetres.

"Mademoiselle Koffi," said a calm voice. "You have a beautiful career ahead of you. It would be such a shame to waste it on rumours. Think about your mother in Daloa. Think about your little brother at university."
The car drove away before she could see the number plate.

She did not sleep that night. At three o'clock in the morning, she sat on her bed, her laptop on her knees, the cursor blinking at the end of her article. She thought about the children with skin rashes. She thought about the old man and his plastic bag. And she thought, too, about her mother, who had sold vegetables for twenty years so that Nadège could study.
Courage, she realised, was not the absence of fear. It was deciding that something else mattered more.

The article was published on Monday under the headline *Gold, Mercury and Silence: Who Protects the Hiré Mine?* By noon, it had been shared fifty thousand times. By the evening, two international news agencies had contacted the newspaper. By Wednesday, the Minister of Mines had announced an official investigation, and Honoré Gnagbo had been "temporarily suspended from his functions".
Nadège received messages of support from strangers all over the country — and a few messages that she preferred to forward to a lawyer without reading twice.

Three weeks later, she went back to Hiré. The excavators were gone. The tent was gone. A team from the ministry was taking samples of the water, and a doctor from a humanitarian organisation had set up a small clinic under a mango tree to examine the children.
Bamba Seydou welcomed her with a bowl of foutou and a smile that, this time, held no pain.
"The river will take years to heal," he said. "Maybe longer than I have left. But at least now it has a chance."
Nadège looked at the water, still faintly orange, still flowing.
"Do you know what surprised me most?" she said. "Everybody knew. The villagers, the gendarmes, the buyers in town. The only thing missing was someone willing to say it out loud."
The old man nodded slowly.

"Gold is heavy, my daughter," he said. "It makes people bend. It makes them silent. But the truth is heavier still — for those who carry it alone." He refilled her bowl. "You helped us carry it. That's all a journalist needs to do."

On the bus back to Abidjan, Nadège opened her notebook and wrote the first line of her next investigation. She had, after all, discovered that she was not afraid — or rather, that she was afraid, and would keep going anyway.
